## Design showcase

This page is a public design and publishing demonstration for feedback, using
placeholder prose and entirely synthetic data. It is not a finished research
article and makes no investment claims. The examples
execute locally with R, knitr, ggplot2, DT, and Plotly.
:::

## Executable R and inline results {#sec-computation}

```{r}
#| label: setup-demo
#| include: false
source("../../R/plot-theme.R")
set.seed(42)
n_obs <- 252L
research <- data.frame(
  day = seq_len(n_obs),
  innovation = rnorm(n_obs, mean = 0, sd = 1)
)
research$path <- cumsum(research$innovation)
palette <- blechturm_palette("light")
plot_accent <- palette$series[[1]]
paper <- palette$paper
ink <- palette$ink
```

This paragraph contains evaluated R: the example has
`r nrow(research)` observations, with a sample mean of
`r format(mean(research$innovation), digits = 3)`.
The values are computed from the same data used in @fig-path and @tbl-summary.
R itself is documented by @R.

### Annotated code

The explanations stay below the code on every screen size. Select a numbered
explanation to highlight its line; copy the code using the separate toolbar.

```{r}
#| label: annotated-example
#| code-fold: false
centered <- research$innovation - mean(research$innovation) # <1>
round(sd(centered), 3) # <2>
```

1. Subtract the sample mean from every simulated observation.
2. Compute the sample standard deviation and print a compact result.

## Figures and cross-references {#sec-figures}

```{r}
#| label: fig-path
#| fig-cap: "An accumulated sequence of simulated normal draws."
#| fig-alt: "A navy line showing the cumulative sum of 252 simulated normal observations."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(research, aes(day, path)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = palette$muted, linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(colour = plot_accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "Observation", y = "Cumulative sum") +
  theme_blechturm("light")
```

@fig-path is numbered automatically. Click the image to try the lightbox.
A cross-reference such as @sec-computation also follows the section if it moves.

### Side-by-side figures

```{r}
#| label: fig-diagnostics
#| fig-cap: "Two diagnostic views of the synthetic observations."
#| fig-subcap: ["Distribution", "Normal Q-Q plot"]
#| fig-alt:
#|   - "A histogram of simulated normal observations."
#|   - "A normal quantile plot of the same observations, with a reference line."
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 3.5
par(
  bg = paper, fg = ink,
  col.axis = ink, col.lab = ink,
  mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1)
)
hist(research$innovation, breaks = 20, col = plot_accent,
     border = paper, main = "", xlab = "Innovation", ylab = "Count")
qqnorm(research$innovation, main = "", pch = 16, cex = 0.6, col = plot_accent)
qqline(research$innovation, col = ink)
```

## A shared plotting palette {#sec-plot-themes}

The ledgr logo supplies the navy, blue, orange, and gray color families.
Orange is darkened for contrast on a light background, while the blues are
lightened for dark mode. The synthetic signals deliberately overlap;
line styles and labels identify them independently of color. These examples
demonstrate the layout, not research findings.

<div class="palette-key">
<span class="palette-navy">Navy</span>
<span class="palette-blue">Blue</span>
<span class="palette-orange">Orange</span>
<span class="palette-graphite">Graphite</span>
</div>

### ggplot2: the static figure

This figure switches between two pre-rendered images when you change the
site's light/dark setting. R runs at render time, never in the browser.

```{r}
#| label: prepare-themed-signals
#| include: false
set.seed(1729)
signals <- expand.grid(
  day = seq_len(60),
  series = factor(c("A", "B", "C", "D"), levels = c("A", "B", "C", "D"))
)
signals$value <- sin(signals$day / 9 + as.integer(signals$series) * 0.4) +
  rnorm(nrow(signals), sd = 0.08)
signal_plot <- ggplot(signals, aes(day, value, colour = series, linetype = series)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("solid", "dashed", "dotted", "dotdash")) +
  labs(x = "Observation", y = "Synthetic signal")
```

::: {.plot-light}

```{r}
#| label: themed-ggplot-light
#| fig-alt: "Four synthetic signals A through D, distinguished by navy, blue, orange and gray colors and different line patterns, on a light background."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5
signal_plot +
  scale_colour_blechturm("light") +
  theme_blechturm("light")
```

:::

::: {.plot-dark}

```{r}
#| label: themed-ggplot-dark
#| fig-alt: "The same four synthetic signals with lighter navy, blue, orange and gray colors and different line patterns, on a charcoal background."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5
signal_plot +
  scale_colour_blechturm("dark") +
  theme_blechturm("dark")
```

:::

### Deliberate emphasis {#sec-plot-focus}

This version deliberately emphasizes **A**, using the same navy accent.
B, C, and D use graphite and retain their distinct line styles. This treatment
suits a question about one focal series; the full palette above gives each
series its own color.

::: {.plot-light}

```{r}
#| label: focused-ggplot-light
#| fig-alt: "Four overlapping synthetic signals; A is navy and the three comparison series are gray, with different line styles, on a light background."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5
p <- blechturm_palette("light")
focus_colours <- setNames(rep(p$muted, 4), levels(signals$series))
focus_colours["A"] <- p$series[[1]]
signal_plot +
  scale_colour_manual(values = focus_colours) +
  theme_blechturm("light")
```

:::

::: {.plot-dark}

```{r}
#| label: focused-ggplot-dark
#| fig-alt: "The same overlapping signals; A is light blue and comparison series are gray, with different line styles, on a charcoal background."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5
p <- blechturm_palette("dark")
focus_colours <- setNames(rep(p$muted, 4), levels(signals$series))
focus_colours["A"] <- p$series[[1]]
signal_plot +
  scale_colour_manual(values = focus_colours) +
  theme_blechturm("dark")
```

:::

### Plotly: the interactive companion

Hover to inspect a value, drag to zoom, double-click to reset, or click a
legend entry to hide a series. The same page theme switch updates chart
backgrounds, text, and trace colors without recomputing the data.

```{r}
#| label: themed-plotly
#| fig-height: 6
p <- plotly::plot_ly()
series_names <- levels(signals$series)
line_styles <- c("solid", "dash", "dot", "dashdot")
for (i in seq_along(series_names)) {
  rows <- signals$series == series_names[i]
  p <- plotly::add_trace(
    p, x = signals$day[rows], y = signals$value[rows],
    name = series_names[i], type = "scatter", mode = "lines",
    line = list(color = palette$series[[i]], dash = line_styles[i], width = 2),
    hovertemplate = "Observation %{x}<br>Signal %{y:.2f}<extra>%{fullData.name}</extra>"
  )
}
p <- plotly::layout(p, xaxis = list(title = "Observation"),
                    yaxis = list(title = "Synthetic signal"))
plotly_blechturm(p)
```

::: {.column-margin}
**Two renderers, one palette.** The static version remains useful in feeds and
documents. Plotly provides inspection controls within this static website.
:::

## Market data from ledgr {#sec-market-data}

These examples use an exported slice of **ledgr_demo_bars**, the bundled
synthetic OHLCV dataset in the local ledgr repository. The seven source fields
are `ts_utc`, `instrument_id`, `open`, `high`, `low`, `close`, and `volume`.

```{r}
#| label: prepare-market-bars
#| include: false
source("../../R/market-plots.R")
market_bars <- read_market_bars("data/ledgr-demo-bars.csv")
visible_bars <- tail(market_bars, 30)
```

The extract contains `r nrow(market_bars)` observations for
`r unique(market_bars$instrument_id)`. The static comparisons show its last
`r nrow(visible_bars)` rows. Prices and volumes come from the same observations
in every chart. These are synthetic price units, with no corporate-action
adjustment applied.

The timestamps retain their UTC values. They are synthetic business-day
labels at midnight, rather than exchange session-close timestamps. Calendar
gaps remain visible; no missing bars are filled or assigned zero volume.

[Download the source rows](data/ledgr-demo-bars.csv) or inspect the
[source revision, generator, and file hashes](data/source.json).
These are input-data visualizations; they do not describe a strategy's
performance or execution fills.

**Direction convention:** blue means close is greater than or equal to open;
orange means close is below open. Equal open and close produce a horizontal
doji body. Volume uses the same convention.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### OHLC bars

The vertical stem runs from low to high. The left tick marks open; the right
tick marks close. Volume sits below on the same timestamp axis.

::: {.plot-light}

```{r}
#| label: market-ohlc-light
#| fig-alt: "Thirty synthetic DEMO_01 OHLC bars with open ticks on the left and close ticks on the right, blue for up or flat and orange for down; volume is aligned beneath the prices on a light background."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6.4
plot_market_bars(visible_bars, style = "ohlc", mode = "light")
```

:::

::: {.plot-dark}

```{r}
#| label: market-ohlc-dark
#| fig-alt: "The same thirty OHLC observations and aligned volume panel on a dark background."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6.4
plot_market_bars(visible_bars, style = "ohlc", mode = "dark")
```

:::

### Filled candles

The body spans open to close and the wick spans low to high. Both directions
use filled bodies here.

::: {.plot-light}

```{r}
#| label: market-filled-light
#| fig-alt: "Thirty synthetic DEMO_01 filled candlesticks, blue for close at or above open and orange for close below open, with aligned volume on a light background."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6.4
plot_market_bars(visible_bars, style = "filled", mode = "light")
```

:::

::: {.plot-dark}

```{r}
#| label: market-filled-dark
#| fig-alt: "The same thirty filled candlesticks and volume observations on a dark background."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6.4
plot_market_bars(visible_bars, style = "filled", mode = "dark")
```

:::

### Hollow candles

Up bodies are hollow with blue outlines; down bodies are filled orange.
The hollow/filled distinction supplements color.

::: {.plot-light}

```{r}
#| label: market-hollow-light
#| fig-alt: "Thirty synthetic DEMO_01 candles with hollow blue up bodies and filled orange down bodies, wicks for high and low, and aligned volume on a light background."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6.4
plot_market_bars(visible_bars, style = "hollow", mode = "light")
```

:::

::: {.plot-dark}

```{r}
#| label: market-hollow-dark
#| fig-alt: "The same hollow and filled candlesticks with aligned volume on a dark background."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6.4
plot_market_bars(visible_bars, style = "hollow", mode = "dark")
```

:::

:::

### Interactive candles and volume {#sec-market-interactive}

This chart contains all 60 source observations and initially displays the
last 30. Hover over or tap a candle to inspect its OHLC values and volume.
Zoom or pan to inspect the earlier observations. The price and volume
panels share the UTC timestamp axis.

```{r}
#| label: market-interactive
#| fig-height: 7.5
market_candles_widget(market_bars, visible = 30)
```

## Tables, static and interactive {#sec-tables}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Descriptive statistics for the synthetic observations."
summary_table <- data.frame(
  Statistic = c("Count", "Mean", "Standard deviation", "Minimum", "Maximum"),
  Value = c(nrow(research), mean(research$innovation), sd(research$innovation),
            min(research$innovation), max(research$innovation))
)
knitr::kable(summary_table, digits = 3, align = c("l", "r"))
```

@tbl-summary is a regular HTML table, suitable for copying and reading in RSS.

### An R htmlwidget

This second table runs entirely in the browser after rendering. Try sorting a
column, searching, or changing pages. It does not need an R server.

```{r}
#| label: interactive-table
#| code-fold: true
DT::datatable(
  transform(research, innovation = round(innovation, 3), path = round(path, 3)),
  rownames = FALSE,
  class = "compact stripe hover",
  width = "100%",
  options = list(pageLength = 5, lengthChange = FALSE, scrollX = TRUE)
)
```

A static table remains useful when an interactive widget is unavailable in a
feed reader, PDF, or other non-browser output.
